script.opening: "Doctor, I've been beside myself since I saw 'abnormal bone' on the app. My X-ray's shown something wrong with the bone in my hip, hasn't it? My brother had cancer that went to his bones, and that's all I can think — is this that? Is it spread from somewhere? I need you to be straight with me. Have I got bone cancer?"

facts.text: If asked: a dull ache in the right hip and lower back for about a year, worse at night and after a day in the garden. It has not suddenly got worse. "It's more of a nag than a pain."
Occasional dull headaches. "Funny thing — my flat cap feels tighter than it used to." Your hearing "isn't what it was" but you put that down to age and machinery.
No weight loss, appetite good, no night sweats, no lumps you have found, no coughing up blood, waterworks and bowels normal for you. You feel well in yourself.
You read the X-ray report on the NHS app two days ago: "abnormal bone" and "Paget's" — you did not know what Paget's meant and assumed it was a type of cancer. You also saw "ALP raised".
Nothing significant. No regular tablets; paracetamol now and then. No allergies.
Retired joiner, 71. Married to Jean. Ex-smoker (stopped 20 years ago). A couple of pints at the weekend. Still drives and does all the garden.

facts.topic: Your brother — hold back until asked
facts.text: Your younger brother Alan died three years ago from prostate cancer that "went into his bones — his hips, his spine". You watched him go downhill fast. Say this only if the doctor asks why you are so frightened, or what you know about bone cancer.
You have not told Jean you looked at the result: "I didn't want to frighten her until I knew." Admit this only if asked who knows or who is supporting you.

Anxious and blunt; you want a straight answer early. If the doctor waffles or gives a lecture before answering, interrupt: "Sorry, but is it cancer or not?" If they say clearly it is not cancer and explain why your symptoms fit, you visibly relax and become curious ("So what is Paget's, then?"). Then you may mention Alan.

ice.ideas: "The X-ray says abnormal bone — I think it's cancer, or cancer that's spread like Alan's did."
ice.concerns: "I watched my brother die when it got into his bones. I can't do that to Jean." You have not told her you saw the result.
ice.expectations: "I want a straight answer — is it cancer?" Then you want to know what happens next and whether it can be treated.

cues: "My brother had cancer that went to his bones." — say in the opening.
"Funny thing, my cap feels tighter these days." — mention when asked about other symptoms.
"I haven't told Jean." — say quietly near the end if asked about home or support.

checkpoints.text: Explains the diagnosis confidently and unfrighteningly: the X-ray changes plus isolated raised ALP (normal calcium) are typical of PAGET’S DISEASE of bone — a common, BENIGN disorder of bone turnover — NOT bone cancer and NOT metastases

Uses his own symptoms to make it make sense: bony aching, headache, and the hat feeling tighter (bony enlargement, e.g. skull) are classic Paget’s features — turning frightening symptoms into a coherent, benign explanation

Outlines the plan: confirm/characterise (Paget’s Association guideline, 2019: total ALP with liver function tests — a normal GGT supports a bone source — plus calcium and vitamin D; a radionuclide bone scan with targeted X-rays to map active disease), treat bone pain due to Paget’s with a bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid most likely to give a good pain response; treatment is symptom-directed, not aimed at normalising ALP), correct low calcium or vitamin D before any bisphosphonate, analgesia, and monitor; explains it is manageable

Mentions relevant complications proportionately WITHOUT eclipsing the reassurance: possible hearing loss if the skull base is involved, fracture risk, rarely deformity, and very rarely malignant change — framed as reasons for monitoring, not as new threats
Addresses the portal-misreading directly: acknowledges how alarming raw report wording is when seen before explanation, and corrects "abnormal bone" → a specific benign condition
Answers the real question ("is it cancer?") clearly and early; surfaces and acknowledges the brother-grief that is driving the terror, with compassion
Checks understanding and the unspoken fears (death sentence; not telling his wife), and offers to involve his wife; leaves him reassured rather than half-reassured

Safety-nets and follows up: what symptoms to report (new hearing change, worsening/rapidly increasing pain, a lump, fracture), the bloods/treatment/monitoring plan, and a review to confirm understanding and response — a clear, calming plan

worked.txt: "Let me answer your question straight away, because you’ve been carrying it: no, this is not bone cancer, and it is not cancer that’s spread. What your X-ray shows is a condition called Paget’s disease of bone. It’s common in people your age, it’s benign — not cancer — and it’s very manageable. Take a breath; you can put the worst fear down."

"And actually it explains things you’ve noticed. In Paget’s, the bone renews itself in a slightly disorganised, overactive way, so the bone can thicken and enlarge a little. That’s why your hat feels tighter, why you get the odd headache, and the aching in your hip. Those aren’t sinister — they’re the condition itself, and they’re treatable."

"I’m sorry the app showed you ‘abnormal bone’ before anyone could explain it — those raw report words are written for doctors, not to be read cold at midnight, and they send people’s minds straight to the worst place. ‘Abnormal’ here just means ‘not the usual pattern’, and the pattern it IS is this benign condition."

"Can I just say — you mentioned your brother, his cancer going to his bones. I think that’s why your mind went straight there, and that’s completely understandable; you’ve seen what that looked like. I’m sorry you lost him. But this is a genuinely different thing, and I can tell you that with confidence."

"Here’s what we do. A couple of blood tests to confirm and see how active it is, sometimes a bone scan to see which bones are involved. If it’s causing you pain, there’s a very effective treatment — usually a bisphosphonate, often a single infusion — plus simple pain relief. Then we keep an eye on a blood marker over time. Most people do very well."

"A few things to tell me about, just so you know: if your hearing changes, if the pain gets much worse or a new lump appears, or you have a fall and think you’ve broken something — those we’d check. Otherwise this is a watch-and-treat condition, not an emergency. And — have you told your wife about the result? It might help to have her in the next chat; you don’t need to carry the scare, or the reassurance, on your own. I’ll see you to go through the bloods. You came in fearing the worst; the truth is a great deal kinder."

f.learning: An incidental X-ray reported as Paget’s disease, with an isolated raised (bone-specific) ALP and normal calcium, is a benign disorder of bone remodelling — NOT bone cancer or metastases. The first and central task is a CONFIDENT benign diagnosis that answers the patient’s real question ("is it cancer?") clearly and early, using his own classic symptoms (bony ache, headache, the hat feeling tighter from bony enlargement) to make the benign explanation cohere. The plan is to confirm/characterise (ALP with liver function tests, calcium, vitamin D, and a radionuclide bone scan to map the disease — Paget’s Association guideline, Ralston et al., JBMR 2019), treat bone pain with a bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid most likely to help; symptom-directed rather than treating the ALP number) plus analgesia, and monitor; complications (skull-base hearing loss, fracture, rare sarcomatous change) are mentioned proportionately as reasons to monitor, not as new threats. The examinable hidden agenda is a brother who died of cancer that "went to the bones", onto which he has pattern-matched a raw portal phrase ("abnormal bone") read before any explanation. Address the portal misreading, acknowledge the brother-grief, check the unspoken death-sentence fear, offer to involve his wife, and safety-net — leaving him fully, not half, reassured. Paget’s is benign and treatable; symptomatic disease is managed with bisphosphonates, and monitored. Rare complications (deafness if skull base involved, fractures, very rarely sarcomatous change — emphasise rare) need awareness but should not dominate the reassurance.

knowledge.guideline: Paget’s Association clinical guideline (Ralston et al., JBMR 2019) · MHRA Drug Safety Update (July 2015) · GMC Good Medical Practice (2024)
knowledge.summary: Typical radiology with an isolated raised ALP and normal calcium is Paget’s disease of bone: common, benign and treatable. Answer “is it cancer?” clearly and early, explain his own symptoms with it, and plan confirmation, symptom-led treatment and monitoring.

points.t: A focal disorder of overactive, disorganised bone remodelling in older adults. Affected bone is enlarged and thickened but structurally weaker. Common sites are the pelvis, spine, skull, femur and tibia. Often found incidentally on an X-ray or a raised ALP.

The report describes the characteristic pattern (cortical thickening, coarse trabeculae, expansion) with no aggressive or destructive features, and calcium is normal. Metastases and primary bone tumours look and behave differently. Where the picture is not typical, the specialist decides on further imaging.

Paget’s Association guideline (2019): total ALP with liver function tests as the first-line biochemical test (a normal GGT supports a bone source), and a radionuclide bone scan with targeted X-rays to define the extent of active disease. Check calcium and vitamin D before any bisphosphonate.

Paget’s Association guideline (2019): bisphosphonates are recommended for bone pain due to Paget’s, with zoledronic acid the most likely to give a good pain response; symptom-directed treatment is preferred over treating to normalise ALP. Simple analgesia for pain; secondary osteoarthritis may need its own treatment.

Hearing loss when the skull is involved, bone deformity, fracture, secondary osteoarthritis and, rarely, nerve compression. Sarcomatous change is rare; new, rapidly worsening pain or a swelling at an affected site needs prompt review.

Correct low vitamin D and calcium first to reduce post-infusion hypocalcaemia. A transient flu-like reaction is common after the first infusion. MHRA Drug Safety Update (July 2015): IV bisphosphonates carry a risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw — patient reminder card, dental check-ups and good oral hygiene.

model.text: Hello Mr Pyle, I’m one of the GPs. I can see you’ve been worried about your X-ray. Tell me what you’ve seen and what’s been going through your mind.
model.why: Invites his understanding and emotion first

model.text: I saw “abnormal bone” on the app. My brother had cancer that went to his bones, and that’s all I can think about. Be straight with me — have I got bone cancer?

I will be completely straight with you, and I’ll answer that first. No — this is not bone cancer, and it is not cancer that has spread. Your X-ray shows a condition called Paget’s disease of bone. It’s common at your age, it’s benign, and it’s treatable.
model.why: Answers the real question clearly and early

model.text: (exhales) You’re sure?

The report describes the typical pattern of Paget’s and specifically no features of anything aggressive, and your calcium is normal. I’ll explain it properly, then ask you a few questions and agree a plan. Is that alright?
model.why: Gives the basis for confidence and sets the agenda

model.text: Tell me about the hip ache — where is it, and what’s it like?
A dull ache in the hip, on and off. It’s what sent me for the X-ray.
Anything else you’ve noticed? Headaches, changes in your hearing, anything feeling different in shape?
model.why: Asks about skull involvement and deformity

model.text: Odd headache. And my hat feels tighter than it used to — I thought I was imagining it.
Any weight loss, night sweats, pain that wakes you at night, or new lumps anywhere?
model.why: Screens for features that would suggest malignancy

model.text: No weight loss. Nothing like that.
With the headaches, any tenderness of your scalp, pain in the jaw when chewing, or change in your vision?
model.why: Excludes giant cell arteritis as a cause of new headache at 71

model.text: No, nothing like that.
You mentioned your brother. Would you tell me about him?
His cancer went to his bones. The pain at the end… When I saw “abnormal bone”, I thought, that’s it, that’s me next.
I’m very sorry you lost him, and that you went through that. It makes complete sense your mind went straight there. Have you been carrying this on your own?
model.why: Acknowledges grief and probes for the unspoken

model.text: I haven’t told my wife I saw it. I didn’t want to frighten her until I knew.

That’s a lot to hold. I’m sorry the app showed you those words before anyone could explain them — they’re written for doctors, and read cold they sound far worse than they are. “Abnormal” here just means “not the usual pattern”.

In Paget’s, the bone renews itself too fast and in a disorganised way, so it becomes thicker and a bit larger. That explains your hip ache, your headaches and your hat feeling tighter — the skull can be involved too. These aren’t signs of cancer; they’re the condition itself.
model.why: Uses his own symptoms to make the benign diagnosis make sense

model.text: So the hat thing is part of it? That’s almost a relief.

Exactly. It needs keeping an eye on — sometimes it can affect hearing if it’s in the skull, or make a bone more likely to break — which is why we monitor it. Very rarely it changes in a way that needs checking, so a new, rapidly worsening pain or a lump is something I’d want to know about. But the outlook for most people is very good.

Here’s what I’d suggest. A blood test to confirm the ALP is from bone and to check your calcium and vitamin D. I’d also refer you to the bone specialists, who often do a bone scan to see which bones are involved.
And treatment?

If it’s causing pain, there’s an effective treatment — usually a drip of a bone-strengthening medicine, often just once — plus simple painkillers meanwhile. The specialists will decide on that with you. I’d also like your hearing checked if you notice any change.
model.why: Symptom-led treatment plan and hearing surveillance

model.text: That’s a lot less frightening than what I’d imagined.
Would it help to have your wife with you when we go through the bloods? You don’t need to carry the scare, or the good news, on your own.
Yes. I think I’ll tell her tonight.

Contact us if your hearing changes, the pain gets much worse quickly, you notice a lump over a bone, or you have a fall and think you’ve broken something. Otherwise, bloods this week and I’ll see you both with the results. When you tell your wife tonight, what will you say?
model.why: Specific safety-net, dated follow-up and teach-back

model.text: That it’s not cancer. It’s Paget’s — the bone renews too fast. Bloods, a scan, maybe a drip. And we come back together.

social.t: His brother’s death from cancer that spread to bone shapes how he reads every result. Acknowledging the loss is part of the reassurance.
He has not told his wife he saw the result. Offer a joint follow-up so neither the scare nor the reassurance is carried alone.

legal.t: Patients can see results and letters through online record access, often before a clinician has explained them. Practices should have a process for results that are likely to cause alarm.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): give information in a way the patient can understand, and be honest about uncertainty without creating false alarm. Here the uncertainty is small and should be described as such.
Record the explanation given, his concerns about cancer, the plan for bloods and referral, and the safety-net.

community.t: Paget’s Association (patient information and helpline); Cruse Bereavement Support if grief for his brother resurfaces.

Weight loss, night pain or new lumps — reconsider malignancy
New headache at 71 with scalp tenderness, jaw claudication or visual change — giant cell arteritis

playbook.diagnosis: Paget’s disease of bone affecting the pelvis, with raised bone-source ALP and normal calcium; headache and a tighter hat suggest skull involvement. Benign; no radiological features of malignancy.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “It’s not cancer. It’s Paget’s disease — the bone renews itself too fast and a bit untidily, so it gets thicker and larger. That’s why your hip aches and your hat feels tighter. It’s treatable and we keep an eye on it.”

management.reflectIce: “You were afraid this was what happened to your brother. I can tell you with confidence it isn’t.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge his grief, apologise for the unexplained app result, and offer to see him with his wife.
sharedPlan: Bloods: ALP with LFTs (GGT), calcium, vitamin D, renal function
Referral to the bone specialists; radionuclide bone scan to map active disease
Symptom-led treatment: zoledronic acid for bone pain after calcium and vitamin D are replete; simple analgesia meanwhile
safetyNet: Report hearing change, rapidly worsening pain, a lump over bone, or a suspected fracture
Review with results, with his wife if he wishes

pitfalls.intro: This station tests results communication. The diagnosis is benign and the evidence is clear, so candidates fail by hedging, by frightening him with rare complications, or by never reaching his brother.

items.fail: Gathering a full history before answering “is it cancer?”.
items.why: He cannot listen until the question is answered; “does not respond to the patient’s agenda”.
items.fix: Answer in the first minute: “No, it isn’t cancer — it’s Paget’s disease”, then explain.

items.fail: Hedging: “we can’t rule anything out until the scan”.
items.why: The report and bloods support a confident benign diagnosis; hedging leaves him half-reassured.
items.fix: Give the basis for confidence: typical pattern, no aggressive features, normal calcium.

items.fail: Leading with osteosarcoma and fracture risk.
items.why: Rare complications eclipse the reassurance and rebuild the fear.
items.fix: Mention complications as reasons for monitoring, after the benign explanation.

items.fail: Treating to normalise ALP, or starting treatment without checking calcium and vitamin D.
items.why: The Paget’s Association guideline (2019) favours symptom-led treatment; low vitamin D raises the risk of hypocalcaemia after zoledronic acid.
items.fix: Bloods first, specialist referral, bisphosphonate for bone pain.

items.fail: Never exploring the brother or the wife.
items.why: The hidden agenda is grief and secrecy; missing it loses the Relating domain.
items.fix: “You mentioned your brother — would you tell me about him?” Then offer a joint follow-up.

items.fail: Using jargon: “isolated raised ALP, pagetic changes, sclerotic lesions”.
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: Plain words: “the bone renews itself too fast and a bit untidily”.

timeMap.d: He asks directly about cancer. Say no, clearly, name Paget’s, and give the reason for your confidence.
Hip ache, headache, the tighter hat, hearing; weight loss, night pain, lumps; GCA symptoms for new headache.
His brother’s bone metastases, the result read alone, the wife not told. Acknowledge grief and the portal shock.
Paget’s explained through his own symptoms; complications in proportion; bloods, specialist referral, bone scan, symptom-led zoledronic acid.
Hearing change, rapid pain, lump, fracture. Offer to see him with his wife. Teach-back.

wordPics.fail: Hedges on the cancer question (“we can’t rule anything out yet”) or leads with osteosarcoma risk; never asks about the brother; offers bloods with no explanation of Paget’s; no plan or safety-net.
wordPics.pass: States clearly it is Paget’s, not cancer; explains what Paget’s is; plans bloods and referral; mentions monitoring and gives a safety-net.
wordPics.exc: All of the above, plus: answers the cancer question within the first minute with the reason; links the hat, headache and hip ache to the diagnosis; acknowledges the brother’s death and the app shock; puts complications in proportion; offers to involve his wife; teach-back.

avoid.dont: “We can’t say for certain it isn’t cancer until we’ve done more tests.”
avoid.instead: “No, this is not cancer. The report shows the typical pattern of Paget’s disease and nothing aggressive.”
avoid.why: Hedging leaves him half-reassured when the evidence supports a clear answer.

avoid.dont: “Paget’s can turn into bone cancer, so we’ll need to watch it.”
avoid.instead: “We monitor it, and a new rapidly worsening pain or lump is something I’d want to know about. That’s rare.”
avoid.why: Leading with a rare complication rebuilds the fear you have just taken apart.

avoid.dont: “You shouldn’t read results on the app before we’ve explained them.”
avoid.instead: “I’m sorry you saw those words before anyone could explain them.”
avoid.why: Blaming him for using his record access adds shame to fear.

SCA_STEM.name: Gordon Pyle
pmh: No significant past medical history recorded
SCA_STEM.recent: Pelvis and hip X-ray for hip ache: changes consistent with Paget’s disease of bone (cortical thickening, coarse trabeculae, bony expansion); no aggressive or destructive features. Bloods: raised ALP, calcium normal. Result visible to him on the patient app before any clinician contact.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video appointment: “worried about my X-ray result”.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: Paget’s Association clinical guideline (Ralston et al., JBMR 2019) · MHRA Drug Safety Update (July 2015) · GMC Good Medical Practice (2024)
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: Typical radiology with an isolated raised ALP and normal calcium is Paget’s disease of bone: common, benign and treatable. Answer “is it cancer?” clearly and early, explain his own symptoms with it, and plan confirmation, symptom-led treatment and monitoring.

points.t: A focal disorder of overactive, disorganised bone remodelling in older adults. Affected bone is enlarged and thickened but structurally weaker. Common sites are the pelvis, spine, skull, femur and tibia. Often found incidentally on an X-ray or a raised ALP.

The report describes the characteristic pattern (cortical thickening, coarse trabeculae, expansion) with no aggressive or destructive features, and calcium is normal. Metastases and primary bone tumours look and behave differently. Where the picture is not typical, the specialist decides on further imaging.

Paget’s Association guideline (2019): total ALP with liver function tests as the first-line biochemical test (a normal GGT supports a bone source), and a radionuclide bone scan with targeted X-rays to define the extent of active disease. Check calcium and vitamin D before any bisphosphonate.

Paget’s Association guideline (2019): bisphosphonates are recommended for bone pain due to Paget’s, with zoledronic acid the most likely to give a good pain response; symptom-directed treatment is preferred over treating to normalise ALP. Simple analgesia for pain; secondary osteoarthritis may need its own treatment.

Hearing loss when the skull is involved, bone deformity, fracture, secondary osteoarthritis and, rarely, nerve compression. Sarcomatous change is rare; new, rapidly worsening pain or a swelling at an affected site needs prompt review.

Correct low vitamin D and calcium first to reduce post-infusion hypocalcaemia. A transient flu-like reaction is common after the first infusion. MHRA Drug Safety Update (July 2015): IV bisphosphonates carry a risk of osteonecrosis of the jaw — patient reminder card, dental check-ups and good oral hygiene.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Invited his account of the app result and his fears before explaining; answered the cancer question early.
Retired joiner; brother’s death from bone metastases; not yet told his wife.
Picked up the brother, the “abnormal bone” phrase and the tighter hat, and used each.
Idea (bone cancer or spread), concern (the same death as his brother), expectation (a straight answer).
ALP with LFTs (GGT), calcium, vitamin D, renal function; specialist referral for radionuclide bone scan; hearing assessment if symptoms.
Paget’s vs metastases vs primary bone tumour vs osteoarthritis; GCA considered for new headache.
Asked about weight loss, night pain, lumps and GCA symptoms; noted the report excluded aggressive features and calcium is normal.
Paget’s disease of the pelvis, with probable skull involvement given the headache and enlarging hat size; benign.
Confirmation bloods, specialist referral, symptom-led bisphosphonate (zoledronic acid) with analgesia; calcium and vitamin D checked first.
Hearing, secondary osteoarthritis, fracture risk and his grief addressed; wife involved with consent.
Report hearing change, rapidly worsening pain, a lump or a fracture; review with results; teach-back.

social.t: His brother’s death from cancer that spread to bone shapes how he reads every result. Acknowledging the loss is part of the reassurance.
He has not told his wife he saw the result. Offer a joint follow-up so neither the scare nor the reassurance is carried alone.

legal.t: Patients can see results and letters through online record access, often before a clinician has explained them. Practices should have a process for results that are likely to cause alarm.

professional.t: GMC Good Medical Practice (2024): give information in a way the patient can understand, and be honest about uncertainty without creating false alarm. Here the uncertainty is small and should be described as such.
Record the explanation given, his concerns about cancer, the plan for bloods and referral, and the safety-net.

community.t: Paget’s Association (patient information and helpline); Cruse Bereavement Support if grief for his brother resurfaces.

redFlags: New, rapidly worsening bone pain or a swelling over affected bone — rare sarcomatous change
Weight loss, night pain or new lumps — reconsider malignancy
New headache at 71 with scalp tenderness, jaw claudication or visual change — giant cell arteritis
psychosocial: Brother died of cancer spread to bone
Saw the result alone on the app; has not told his wife
Retired joiner — activity and function with hip pain
ice: Idea: “Abnormal bone” means bone cancer or cancer that has spread
Concern: dying the way his brother did

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Paget’s disease of bone affecting the pelvis, with raised bone-source ALP and normal calcium; headache and a tighter hat suggest skull involvement. Benign; no radiological features of malignancy.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “It’s not cancer. It’s Paget’s disease — the bone renews itself too fast and a bit untidily, so it gets thicker and larger. That’s why your hip aches and your hat feels tighter. It’s treatable and we keep an eye on it.”

management.reflectIce: “You were afraid this was what happened to your brother. I can tell you with confidence it isn’t.”
management.psychosocial: Acknowledge his grief, apologise for the unexplained app result, and offer to see him with his wife.
sharedPlan: Bloods: ALP with LFTs (GGT), calcium, vitamin D, renal function
Referral to the bone specialists; radionuclide bone scan to map active disease
Symptom-led treatment: zoledronic acid for bone pain after calcium and vitamin D are replete; simple analgesia meanwhile
safetyNet: Report hearing change, rapidly worsening pain, a lump over bone, or a suspected fracture
Review with results, with his wife if he wishes

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests results communication. The diagnosis is benign and the evidence is clear, so candidates fail by hedging, by frightening him with rare complications, or by never reaching his brother.

items.fail: Gathering a full history before answering “is it cancer?”.
items.why: He cannot listen until the question is answered; “does not respond to the patient’s agenda”.
items.fix: Answer in the first minute: “No, it isn’t cancer — it’s Paget’s disease”, then explain.

items.fail: Hedging: “we can’t rule anything out until the scan”.
items.why: The report and bloods support a confident benign diagnosis; hedging leaves him half-reassured.
items.fix: Give the basis for confidence: typical pattern, no aggressive features, normal calcium.

items.fail: Leading with osteosarcoma and fracture risk.
items.why: Rare complications eclipse the reassurance and rebuild the fear.
items.fix: Mention complications as reasons for monitoring, after the benign explanation.

items.fail: Treating to normalise ALP, or starting treatment without checking calcium and vitamin D.
items.why: The Paget’s Association guideline (2019) favours symptom-led treatment; low vitamin D raises the risk of hypocalcaemia after zoledronic acid.
items.fix: Bloods first, specialist referral, bisphosphonate for bone pain.

items.fail: Never exploring the brother or the wife.
items.why: The hidden agenda is grief and secrecy; missing it loses the Relating domain.
items.fix: “You mentioned your brother — would you tell me about him?” Then offer a joint follow-up.

items.fail: Using jargon: “isolated raised ALP, pagetic changes, sclerotic lesions”.
items.why: “Language not easily understood by the patient.”
items.fix: Plain words: “the bone renews itself too fast and a bit untidily”.
